report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Insurance-related differences in post-acute care after critical illness have mostly been studied within single conditions or settings.

We described Medicaid-private differences in discharge destination and length of stay among working-age adults in two non-equivalent settings: 20,511 patients whose first hospitalization included an ICU stay at one Massachusetts academic medical center (2008)(2009)(2010)(2011)(2012)(2013)(2014)(2015)(2016)(2017)(2018)(2019)(2020)(2021)(2022), and 603,512 Texas hospitalizations with ICU or coronary care unit accommodation charges in 325 acute care hospitals (2017-2019).

Adjusted for admission-time characteristics, Medicaid was associated in both settings with more skilled nursing facility discharge (5.2 and 4.3 percentage points), less inpatient rehabilitation (-2.0 and -2.6 points), and longer stays.
Long-term acute care and total facility use differed in direction.
Destination differences persisted with further adjustment and in a common 2017-2019 period; length-of-stay differences narrowed.
Texas Medicaid rules limiting adult freestanding rehabilitation and inpatient days are consistent with, but cannot establish, a role for benefit design.
Survivors of critical illness often leave the hospital with new physical, cognitive, and mental health impairments (Needham et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Survivors of critical illness often leave the hospital with new physical, cognitive, and mental health impairments <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Needham et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Where they go next -home, home with home health care, a skilled nursing facility (SNF), an inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF), or a long-term acute care hospital (LTCH) -determines the setting and intensity of services they receive after discharge.

IRFs provide intensive hospital-level rehabilitation, LTCHs extended hospital care for prolonged critical illness (Kahn, Benson, et al., 2010), and SNFs skilled nursing and therapy at lower intensity.
text.formatted: IRFs provide intensive hospital-level rehabilitation, LTCHs extended hospital care for prolonged critical illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kahn, Benson, et al., 2010)</ref>, and SNFs skilled nursing and therapy at lower intensity.

text.text: Which setting a patient enters depends on clinical need and also on coverage, authorization, and provider acceptance.
Insurance has been associated with post-acute care in several populations.

Among working-age stroke survivors, Medicaid was associated with more institutional post-acute care but, among institutional users, with less IRF and more SNF care (Skolarus et al., 2012), and a national stroke registry found Medicaid patients more likely than privately insured patients to be discharged to an SNF and less likely to an IRF (Medford-Davis et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Among working-age stroke survivors, Medicaid was associated with more institutional post-acute care but, among institutional users, with less IRF and more SNF care <ref type="bibr">(Skolarus et al., 2012)</ref>, and a national stroke registry found Medicaid patients more likely than privately insured patients to be discharged to an SNF and less likely to an IRF <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Medford-Davis et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Among workingage stroke patients with Medicaid in 2010, IRF discharge was less common in states whose Medicaid programs did not cover IRF care, a group that included Texas (Skolarus et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Among workingage stroke patients with Medicaid in 2010, IRF discharge was less common in states whose Medicaid programs did not cover IRF care, a group that included Texas <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Skolarus et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Among mechanically ventilated patients in Pennsylvania, Medicaid was associated with lower LTCH use than commercial insurance (Lane-Fall et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Among mechanically ventilated patients in Pennsylvania, Medicaid was associated with lower LTCH use than commercial insurance <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lane-Fall et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Findings differ across conditions (Kane et al., 2014), and Medicaid expansion has been associated with more rehabilitation after injury (Zogg et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Findings differ across conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kane et al., 2014)</ref>, and Medicaid expansion has been associated with more rehabilitation after injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Zogg et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In the database used here, two recent conference abstracts examined insurance and ICU length of stay among patients with stroke (Shah, 2025) and discharge to inpatient rehabilitation among ICU patients with ischemic stroke treated with thrombolysis (Shah & Strobel, 2026); both concern a single condition and a single outcome and have not been peer reviewed.
text.formatted: In the database used here, two recent conference abstracts examined insurance and ICU length of stay among patients with stroke <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Shah, 2025)</ref> and discharge to inpatient rehabilitation among ICU patients with ischemic stroke treated with thrombolysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Shah & Strobel, 2026)</ref>; both concern a single condition and a single outcome and have not been peer reviewed.

text.text: Insurance may also be related to length of stay: authorization and bed availability are commonly documented reasons for delayed discharge (Sorensen et al., 2020), and among injured patients discharged to facilities, those enrolled in Medicaid retroactively during the admission had longer stays than those with established Medicaid coverage (Haddad et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Insurance may also be related to length of stay: authorization and bed availability are commonly documented reasons for delayed discharge <ref type="bibr">(Sorensen et al., 2020)</ref>, and among injured patients discharged to facilities, those enrolled in Medicaid retroactively during the admission had longer stays than those with established Medicaid coverage <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Haddad et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In Massachusetts, non-peer-reviewed hospital association and state task force reports describe payer authorization, including by commercial insurers, as a source of delayed transitions (Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association, 2025; Massachusetts TACPAC Task Force, 2025).
text.formatted: In Massachusetts, non-peer-reviewed hospital association and state task force reports describe payer authorization, including by commercial insurers, as a source of delayed transitions <ref type="bibr">(Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Massachusetts TACPAC Task Force, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Two gaps remain.

First, most studies concern a single diagnosis or a single post-acute setting, so they cannot show whether insurance is related to whether patients receive facilitybased care, which facility they receive, or both.
Second, single-site or single-state studies cannot show which associations recur across settings that differ in their data, populations, and Medicaid programs.

We therefore described Medicaid-private differences in the full distribution of discharge destinations and in length of stay among working-age survivors of intensive care in two nonequivalent settings: one academic medical center in Massachusetts, a state that expanded Medicaid, and acute care hospitals in Texas, a state that did not (Kaiser Family Foundation & Georgetown University Center for Children and Families, 2019).
text.formatted: We therefore described Medicaid-private differences in the full distribution of discharge destinations and in length of stay among working-age survivors of intensive care in two nonequivalent settings: one academic medical center in Massachusetts, a state that expanded Medicaid, and acute care hospitals in Texas, a state that did not <ref type="bibr">(Kaiser Family Foundation &</ref> Georgetown University Center for Children and Families, 2019).

text.text: We asked which associations were similar across settings and which differed.
We then compared the differences with documented Medicaid benefit rules in each state as a way to generate hypotheses, not to estimate policy effects.
The study adds three things to prior work.

First, it reports every discharge destination separately in a broad, all-diagnosis population of working-age survivors of intensive care, which shows that the most consistent insurance difference concerns the type of post-acute care (nursing facility rather than inpatient rehabilitation) more than the amount of facility-based care; a single facility composite would have obscured offsetting differences.
Earlier analyses of the same database were limited to stroke and to one outcome (Shah, 2025; Shah & Strobel, 2026).
text.formatted: Earlier analyses of the same database were limited to stroke and to one outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Shah, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Shah & Strobel, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Second, it pairs a clinically detailed single-center cohort with a large discharge dataset from 319 Texas hospitals analyzed within hospitals, so that the main associations do not rest on one institution's case mix or referral network.

Third, it documents the Texas Medicaid benefit rules for adult IRF care and inpatient days in force during the study years, including the programs to which they applied, and shows that the Texas pattern is consistent with them, extending stroke-specific evidence on IRF coverage (Skolarus et al., 2014) to critical illness and to LTCH care.
text.formatted: Third, it documents the Texas Medicaid benefit rules for adult IRF care and inpatient days in force during the study years, including the programs to which they applied, and shows that the Texas pattern is consistent with them, extending stroke-specific evidence on IRF coverage <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Skolarus et al., 2014)</ref> to critical illness and to LTCH care.

text.text: The comparison across settings is descriptive and generates hypotheses about benefit design.
We used the behavioral model of health services use, in which use reflects need, predisposing characteristics, and enabling resources (Andersen, 1995).
text.formatted: We used the behavioral model of health services use, in which use reflects need, predisposing characteristics, and enabling resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andersen, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: After critical illness, need is reflected in comorbidity, acute severity, and organ support; predisposing characteristics include age, sex, and race and ethnicity; and insurance is an enabling resource.
We distinguish three ways insurance may be related to post-acute care.
Through benefit design, a payer may not cover a setting for adults or may limit inpatient days.
Through administration, prior authorization and network rules may delay or prevent placement.
Through provider acceptance, facilities may decline a payer's rates.
Other enabling factors, such as caregiver support, housing, and substance use, are correlated with insurance and may independently limit discharge home.
These channels suggest patterns, not tests.
Provider acceptance and social circumstances would be expected to produce less discharge home and more facility use with Medicaid in both settings.

Benefit design would be expected to make the type of facility track a state's rules, with less use of settings that its Medicaid program covers narrowly for adults and substitution toward settings it covers.
Administrative and placement delays would be expected to lengthen hospital stays, particularly among patients discharged to facilities.

Because insurance is recorded at admission and several clinical measures accrue during the stay and may themselves reflect care processes, the framework also orders covariates in time (Figure 1; Supplementary Table S2), which determined the estimand and the sequence of models.
text.formatted: Because insurance is recorded at admission and several clinical measures accrue during the stay and may themselves reflect care processes, the framework also orders covariates in time (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>), which determined the estimand and the sequence of models.

text.text: This was a retrospective, two-setting cohort study with separate data sources and analyses; the settings were not pooled.
Setting 1 is a single academic medical center in Boston, Massachusetts.
Setting 2 is acute care hospitals in Texas that reported to the state discharge data system.
Reporting follows the STROBE and RECORD guidelines (von Elm et al., 2007; Benchimol et al., 2015); the checklist is in Supplementary Table S13.
text.formatted: Reporting follows the STROBE and RECORD guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(von Elm et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Benchimol et al., 2015)</ref>; the checklist is in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S13</ref>.

text.text: We used MIMIC-IV version 3.1 (Johnson, Bulgarelli, Shen, et al., 2023; Johnson, Bulgarelli, Pollard, et al., 2024), de-identified electronic health records for patients admitted to the emergency department or ICUs of the medical center from 2008 to 2022, accessed through PhysioNet (Pollard et al., 2026) under a credentialed data use agreement.
text.formatted: We used MIMIC-IV version 3.1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Johnson, Bulgarelli, Shen, et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Johnson, Bulgarelli, Pollard, et al., 2024)</ref>, de-identified electronic health records for patients admitted to the emergency department or ICUs of the medical center from 2008 to 2022, accessed through PhysioNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pollard et al., 2026)</ref> under a credentialed data use agreement.

text.text: Severity and treatment variables came from the MIMIC Code Repository derived tables (Johnson et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Severity and treatment variables came from the MIMIC Code Repository derived tables <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Johnson et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For each patient we selected the first hospitalization that included an ICU stay, before applying other criteria; the unit of analysis is the patient.

We used the Texas Hospital Inpatient Discharge Public Use Data File (PUDF), which contains discharges reported by state-licensed hospitals; reporting exemptions for rural hospitals were repealed beginning with 2015 data (Texas Department of State Health Services, 2020 , 2021).
text.formatted: We used the Texas Hospital Inpatient Discharge Public Use Data File (PUDF), which contains discharges reported by state-licensed hospitals; reporting exemptions for rural hospitals were repealed beginning with 2015 data <ref type="bibr">(Texas Department of State Health Services, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The primary period was 2017-2019; 2020 was analyzed separately, after removing outpatient records that the state identified in the second-quarter 2020 file.
The PUDF has no patient identifier, so the unit of analysis is the hospitalization.
Eligible stays were hospitalizations with ICU or coronary care unit (CCU) accommodation charges, recorded under revenue centers 020X and 021X (Texas Department of State Health Services, 2020).

The ICU category also includes intermediate (step-down), burn, trauma, and psychiatric intensive care charges, which the file reports as a single amount, so stays with any of these charges enter the cohort and the Texas cohort is a billing-based construct rather than a validated clinical ICU cohort.

We therefore report results separately for stays with ICU charges only and CCU charges only, and after excluding stays in mental health and substance use diagnostic categories and in psychiatric-designated hospitals.
The specialty-unit field cannot serve as an independent check: the ICU or CCU was coded as the first specialty unit for 99% of eligible stays.

In both settings we included adults aged 18-64 years who survived to discharge, were not discharged to hospice, had Medicaid or private insurance, and had a classifiable discharge destination; Setting 1 also required a valid interval between final ICU exit and discharge.
Texas stays at hospitals with masked identifiers or at specialty hospitals without an acute care indicator were excluded.

On Texas records with HIV or substance use diagnoses, the state reports age in coarsened groups (18-44 and 45-64 years) and masks sex; in the primary models these records keep their coarsened age group as its own category and an unknown sex category, and sensitivity analysis S9 excludes them.
Sample flows are shown in Supplementary Figure S1 and, for Texas by payer, Supplementary Table S1.
text.formatted: Sample flows are shown in Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref> and, for Texas by payer, Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>.

text.text: In Setting 1 the exposure was admission-recorded insurance (Medicaid or private).

In Setting 2 it was the expected primary payer on the claim: Medicaid, or private (commercial preferred provider, point-of-service, exclusive provider, indemnity, health maintenance organization, Blue Cross Blue Shield, or other commercial plans); Medicare Advantage claims were classified as Medicare (Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: In Setting 2 it was the expected primary payer on the claim: Medicaid, or private (commercial preferred provider, point-of-service, exclusive provider, indemnity, health maintenance organization, Blue Cross Blue Shield, or other commercial plans); Medicare Advantage claims were classified as Medicare (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Both are administrative labels.

Neither source identifies Medicaid eligibility group, managed care program or plan, or dual eligibility, and some Texas Medicaid managed care claims may be filed under commercial health maintenance organization codes.
The author set the outcomes and their priority before the Texas analyses were run; the hierarchy was not prospectively registered.
The primary outcomes were discharge to an SNF or nursing facility, discharge to an IRF, and hospital length of stay (LOS).

Secondary outcomes were discharge home, with home health care, to an LTCH, to other destinations (against medical advice, transfer to another acute or psychiatric hospital, custodial care, and other), and to any post-acute facility (SNF, IRF, or LTCH).

Destinations are harmonized administrative categories built from different source fields (Supplementary Table S3), not necessarily identical clinical settings; the Texas nursing facility category combines Medicare-certified SNFs and Medicaidonly nursing facilities, which we also report separately.
text.formatted: Destinations are harmonized administrative categories built from different source fields (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>), not necessarily identical clinical settings; the Texas nursing facility category combines Medicare-certified SNFs and Medicaidonly nursing facilities, which we also report separately.

text.text: LOS was measured in both settings as the whole hospital stay in calendar days (discharge date minus admission date, minimum 1), the definition available in Texas.
In Setting 1 only, we also measured days from final ICU exit to hospital discharge (post-ICU days), treating negative intervals of up to 4 hours as zero.
Neither LOS measure identifies time medically ready for discharge, placement delay, or avoidable days.

Admission-time covariates in Setting 1 were age (linear and quadratic), sex, race and ethnicity, admission type, and admission period; in Setting 2 they were age group, sex, race, ethnicity, admission type and source, emergency department use, and discharge quarter.
Comorbidity was measured with the Charlson index without age points (Charlson et al., 1987; Quan et al., 2005).

text.text: Its timing differs by source: MIMIC-IV diagnosis codes are assigned at discharge and carry no present-on-admission indicator, so the Setting 1 index may include conditions that arose during the stay; in Setting 2 we computed the index from all diagnosis codes and, as a check, only from codes flagged as present on admission or exempt from that reporting.

For each outcome, the target quantity is the difference between Medicaid and privately insured patients (Setting 1) or stays (Setting 2) in the probability of each destination, or in mean LOS, standardized to the covariate distribution of the analytic sample -in Texas, among stays in the same hospital.
It is a descriptive association, not the causal effect of insurance.

text.text: Only the admission-time characteristics are clearly measured before insurance could influence care, so the admission-time model (M0) is the primary descriptive comparison.

We then added, in temporal order, comorbidity (M1); organ support (M2); in Texas, discharge-assigned severity of illness, risk of mortality, and major diagnostic category, and in Massachusetts, first-day severity and the ICU course (M3); and diagnosis-coded social-needs proxies (M4).

Because later covariates may lie on pathways from insurance to the outcome or be coded differently by payer, M1-M4 are conditional, postadmission-adjusted associations and do not show whether severity explains a payer difference.
We report M3, the covariate set of the earlier single-center analysis, alongside M0 throughout.

text.text: In Setting 1, 20,511 patients aged 18-64 years met the criteria, of whom 6,934 (33.8%) had Medicaid.

In Setting 2, of 9,339,506 discharges in 2017-2019, 2,479,142 were adult stays with ICU or CCU charges and 1,222,806 were among patients aged 18-64 years; of these, 645,595 had Medicaid or private insurance, most exclusions being stays with Medicare (disability-related), self-pay, or charity coverage.

text.text: Medicaid was associated with longer stays in both settings.

Adjusted for admission-time characteristics, whole-stay LOS was 1.91 days longer in Setting 1 and 1.41 days longer within Texas hospitals; with the full covariate set, the differences were 1.29 days (95% CI, 0.98 to 1.61) and 0.66 days (0.54 to 0.78; ratio of geometric means 1.04).
In Setting 1, Medicaid was also associated with 1.03 more post-ICU days in the two-part model (95% CI, 0.80 to 1.21).

In both settings the LOS difference was larger among patients discharged to a post-acute facility than among those discharged home (Setting 1, 2.30 vs 0.65 post-ICU days; Setting 2, 2.25 [1.42 to 3.08] vs 0.63 [0.54 to 0.72] whole-stay days); because destination may itself depend on insurance, this stratified comparison is descriptive.

In the linear models, the destination associations changed modestly as covariates were added in temporal order (the SNF difference narrowed and the IRF difference widened slightly), whereas the LOS associations narrowed more (Table 5 and Supplementary Table S5).

In a single academic medical center in Massachusetts and 325 acute care hospitals in Texas, Medicaid, compared with private insurance, was associated with a similar pattern among working-age survivors of intensive care: more discharge to nursing facilities, less discharge to inpatient rehabilitation or home without services, and longer hospital stays.
It was present with admission-time adjustment alone and, in Texas, within hospitals, in a bounded-probability model, across charge-defined subgroups, and without dependence on any single hospital.

Destination differences changed modestly but persisted as covariates measured during the stay were added, whereas the LOS differences narrowed by a third to a half with adjustment for comorbidity and severity.
Whether Medicaid patients received more facility-based care differed between settings, because LTCH use was higher with Medicaid in Massachusetts and lower in Texas.

The consistent finding -nursing facility rather than rehabilitation -extends results from working-age and registry stroke populations (Skolarus et al., 2012; Medford-Davis et al., 2016) to a broad, all-diagnosis critical illness population.

It is compatible with the provider-acceptance, administrative, and social channels of the framework, which could operate in both states.
The data cannot show whether the SNF placements were clinically appropriate, whether patients were eligible for or offered IRF care, or how patients fared after discharge.
The differences between settings are consistent with the benefit channel, but the design cannot attribute them to it.

text.text: We could not obtain a 2017 manual, the manual does not address LTCH stays, and the payer field does not identify program, so which stays were subject to which rule is unknown.
The very low Texas ratios for IRF and LTCH discharge, their concentration among ventilated patients, and the relative increases in SNF and home health discharge are consistent with these rules.

In Massachusetts, whose Medicaid regulations provide for chronic disease and rehabilitation hospital services (MassHealth, 2015), the IRF difference was smaller and LTCH use was higher with Medicaid; the regulation does not show that all enrollees had equivalent access to these settings.
The Texas LTCH finding also matches evidence from Pennsylvania (Lane-Fall et al., 2012), where these rules did not apply.

text.text: The contrast therefore motivates a hypothesis -that adult Medicaid benefit design shapes the type of post-acute care after critical illness -that requires designs using policy variation to test.
Eligibility composition also differs.

During the study period, Texas Medicaid covered parents only up to 17% of the federal poverty level and did not cover other nondisabled adults, whereas Massachusetts covered adults up to 138% (Kaiser Family Foundation & Georgetown University Center for Children and Families, 2019).

text.text: Working-age Texas Medicaid patients are therefore more likely to qualify through disability, pregnancy, or extreme poverty, and may have functional and social needs that administrative data do not capture.

This could contribute to the larger Texas differences, although greater need alone would be expected to increase, not decrease, IRF and LTCH use, and excluding pregnancy stays did not change the results.

Longer stays with Medicaid in both settings, concentrated among patients discharged to facilities, are compatible with documented delays in authorization and placement (Sorensen et al., 2020; Haddad et al., 2025) and with Massachusetts reports of payer-related transition delays (Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association, 2025; Massachusetts TACPAC Task Force, 2025), but LOS also reflects severity, complications, and the ICU course -adjustment for these narrowed the differences -and neither data source records when patients were medically ready for discharge.

text.text: The findings have three implications for research and practice, none of which assumes that a shift between settings is harmful.

First, studies of post-acute access should report destinations separately; in Texas, a single facility composite showed little difference by payer while concealing large, offsetting SNF, IRF, and LTCH differences.

Second, adult Medicaid coverage of IRF and LTCH care and inpatient day limits are explicit, documented benefit choices that are consistent with the largest differences here; they merit direct evaluation with designs that exploit changes in these rules, linked to clinical eligibility, program enrollment, and post-discharge outcomes.
Third, hospitals and Medicaid plans could track destination and LOS by payer alongside referral, authorization, and acceptance data to identify which channel operates.
This study has limitations.

The settings are not equivalent in unit of analysis, hospitals, covariates, or measurement, and the Massachusetts common-period subset only approximates 2017-2019, so differences between them cannot be attributed to state policy.
Insurance was measured from administrative records, which may misclassify coverage, program, plan type, and dual eligibility; in Texas, some Medicaid managed care claims may be coded as commercial.
Benefit rules could not be linked to individual stays.

The Texas cohort is defined by billing categories that include intermediate, burn, trauma, and psychiatric intensive care charges, and repeated stays by the same patient cannot be identified, so hospital-clustered errors do not capture dependence among stays by one patient at different hospitals.
Discharge destination fields can misclassify LTCH transfers (Kahn & Iwashyna, 2010), and destinations are harmonized administrative categories.
text.formatted: Discharge destination fields can misclassify LTCH transfers <ref type="bibr">(Kahn & Iwashyna, 2010)</ref>, and destinations are harmonized administrative categories.

text.text: Covariates measured after admission may be affected by care processes, and Massachusetts comorbidity codes lack present-on-admission indicators.
Administrative data lack pre-admission function, caregiver support, and preferences, and the diagnosis-coded social-needs proxies may be incompletely and differentially coded.
We did not observe whether IRF or LTCH care was requested, denied, or declined, or any post-discharge outcomes.
Finally, Setting 1 is a single academic center.

Among working-age survivors of intensive care at a Massachusetts academic medical center and Texas hospitalizations with ICU or coronary care unit accommodation charges, Medicaid was consistently associated with nursing facility rather than rehabilitation discharge and with longer hospital stays, whereas overall facility use differed between settings.
Texas Medicaid rules limiting adult freestanding rehabilitation and, in some programs, inpatient days are consistent with the Texas pattern and warrant direct evaluation.
